title: rjsf 0.0.0.9000
text:
rjsf 0.0.0.9000

Added initial R package skeleton.
Added reticulate bridge to Python jsf.
Added Lotka-Volterra and SIR examples.
Added general jsf_simulate() wrapper.
Added initial JSFResult S7 class, constructor, converter, print, and summary methods.

Michael Lydeamore (author)
rjsf provides an R interface to Jump-Switch-Flow (JSF), a hybrid simulation framework for compartmental models that combines stochastic jump dynamics at low populations with deterministic flow dynamics at high populations.
Important: rjsf is an R interface; running simulations requires the Python Jump-Switch-Flow backend to be installed and accessible through reticulate.
The main function is jsf_simulate(), which lets users define compartmental reaction models in R and return simulation output as either a regular data.frame or a structured JSFResult object.

title: rjsf
text:
Installation
You can install the development version of rjsf from GitHub with:
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("olivervu25/rjsf")

title: rjsf
text:
Python setup
rjsf uses reticulate to call the Python jsf package. This means Python jsf must be installed in the same Python environment that reticulate is using.
A recommended setup is to create a local virtual environment:
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
python -m pip install numpy scipy pandas matplotlib python-libsbml
python -m pip install git+https://github.com/DGermano8/jsf.git
Then in R, point reticulate to that environment:
Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = ".venv/bin/python")

library(reticulate)
py_config()
Check that Python jsf is available:
library(rjsf)

jsf_available()
This should return:
[1] TRUE

title: rjsf
text:
Alternative setup using reticulate
You can also install the Python dependencies from R using reticulate:
library(reticulate)

virtualenv_create("rjsf-env")

py_install(
  packages = c("numpy", "scipy", "pandas", "matplotlib", "python-libsbml"),
  envname = "rjsf-env",
  method = "virtualenv"
)

py_install(
  packages = "git+https://github.com/DGermano8/jsf.git",
  envname = "rjsf-env",
  method = "virtualenv",
  pip = TRUE
)

use_virtualenv("rjsf-env", required = TRUE)
Then check:
library(rjsf)

jsf_available()

title: rjsf
text:
Quick example
The following example simulates a Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system and returns a structured JSFResult object.
library(rjsf)
library(reticulate)

rates_lv <- reticulate::py_eval(
  "lambda x, t: [2.0 * x[0], 1.5 * x[1], 0.05 * x[0] * x[1]]"
)

result <- jsf_simulate(
  x0 = c(prey = 50, predator = 10),
  rates = rates_lv,
  reactant = matrix(
    c(
      1, 0,
      0, 1,
      1, 1
    ),
    ncol = 2,
    byrow = TRUE
  ),
  product = matrix(
    c(
      2, 0,
      0, 0,
      0, 2
    ),
    ncol = 2,
    byrow = TRUE
  ),
  do_disc = c(1, 1),
  t_max = 10,
  dt = 0.01,
  switching_threshold = c(30, 30),
  species_names = c("prey", "predator"),
  return_type = "JSFResult"
)

result
summary(result)
plot(result)

title: rjsf
text:
Output types
jsf_simulate() can return either a regular data frame:
df <- jsf_simulate(..., return_type = "data.frame")
or a structured JSFResult object:
result <- jsf_simulate(..., return_type = "JSFResult")
A JSFResult stores simulation trajectories and metadata, and supports:
print(result)
summary(result)
plot(result)
The simulated prey and predator trajectories can be visualised directly from the JSFResult object:

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
rjsf provides an R interface to the Python jsf package for Jump-Switch-Flow simulation.
The main user-facing function is jsf_simulate(). It lets users:

Define a compartmental reaction model in R.
Pass the model to the Python jsf backend through reticulate.
Return the simulation output as either:

a regular R data.frame; or
a structured JSFResult object.


A JSFResult object supports standard methods such as:

print(result)
summary(result)
plot(result)

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
Set up Python jsf
rjsf uses reticulate to communicate with Python. The Python jsf package must therefore be installed in the same Python environment used by reticulate.
One option is to install the dependencies from R:

install.packages("reticulate")

reticulate::virtualenv_create("rjsf-env")

reticulate::py_install(
  packages = c(
    "numpy",
    "python-libsbml",
    "ipykernel"
  ),
  envname = "rjsf-env",
  method = "virtualenv"
)

reticulate::py_install(
  packages = "git+https://github.com/DGermano8/jsf.git",
  envname = "rjsf-env",
  method = "virtualenv",
  pip = TRUE
)

reticulate::use_virtualenv(
  "rjsf-env",
  required = TRUE
)

You can inspect the Python environment selected by reticulate with:

reticulate::py_config()

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
Check Python jsf
Load rjsf and check whether the Python jsf module is available:

library(rjsf)

jsf_available()

A correctly configured environment should return:
[1] TRUE
If it returns FALSE, check that:

Python jsf is installed;
it is installed in the environment currently used by reticulate; and
reticulate::py_config() reports the expected Python executable.

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
Lotka–Volterra predator–prey model
The Lotka–Volterra model describes interactions between two species:

prey;
predator.

The model contains three reactions:

Prey birth: Prey -> 2 Prey
Predator death: Predator -> ∅
Predation: Prey + Predator -> 2 Predator

The state vector is:

x <- c(prey, predator)


Define the rate function
The Python jsf backend expects the rate function to be a Python callable. We create one using reticulate::py_eval():

rates_lv <- reticulate::py_eval(
  "lambda x, t: [2.0 * x[0], 1.5 * x[1], 0.05 * x[0] * x[1]]"
)

The three rates correspond to:
2.0 * prey                # prey birth
1.5 * predator            # predator death
0.05 * prey * predator    # predation


Define the stoichiometry
The reactant matrix describes what each reaction consumes:

reactant_lv <- matrix(
  c(
    1, 0,
    0, 1,
    1, 1
  ),
  ncol = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

reactant_lv

The product matrix describes what each reaction produces:

product_lv <- matrix(
  c(
    2, 0,
    0, 0,
    0, 2
  ),
  ncol = 2,
  byrow = TRUE
)

product_lv

Internally, jsf_simulate() calculates the net stoichiometry matrix as:
nu = product - reactant
For this model, the net state changes are:
Prey -> 2 Prey                 [+1,  0]
Predator -> ∅                  [ 0, -1]
Prey + Predator -> 2 Predator  [-1, +1]


Run the simulation
Run the model and request a JSFResult object:

result_lv <- jsf_simulate(
  x0 = c(prey = 50, predator = 10),
  rates = rates_lv,
  reactant = reactant_lv,
  product = product_lv,
  do_disc = c(1, 1),
  t_max = 10,
  dt = 0.01,
  switching_threshold = c(30, 30),
  species_names = c("prey", "predator"),
  return_type = "JSFResult"
)

The important arguments are:

x0 defines the initial number of prey and predators.
do_disc = c(1, 1) allows both species to be treated discretely when required.
switching_threshold = c(30, 30) defines the switching threshold for each species.
return_type = "JSFResult" returns a structured result containing the simulation trajectory and associated metadata.



Inspect the result
Print the result:

result_lv

Calculate a summary:

summary(result_lv)

Plot the simulated trajectories:

plot(result_lv)

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
SIR epidemic model
The SIR model describes the spread of an infectious disease through three compartments:

S: susceptible;
I: infectious;
R: recovered.

The model contains two reactions:

Infection: S + I -> 2 I
Recovery: I -> R

The state vector is:

x <- c(S, I, R)


Define the model parameters
Set the total population, infection rate, and recovery rate:

N <- 1000
beta <- 0.5
gamma <- 0.1

Here:
N      = total population
beta   = infection rate
gamma  = recovery rate


Define the rate function
Create a Python callable containing the infection and recovery rates:

rates_sir <- reticulate::py_eval(sprintf(
  "lambda x, t: [%f * x[0] * x[1] / %f, %f * x[1]]",
  beta,
  N,
  gamma
))

The rates correspond to:
beta * S * I / N    # infection
gamma * I           # recovery


Define the stoichiometry
Define the reactant matrix:

reactant_sir <- matrix(
  c(
    1, 1, 0,
    0, 1, 0
  ),
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

reactant_sir

Define the product matrix:

product_sir <- matrix(
  c(
    0, 2, 0,
    0, 0, 1
  ),
  ncol = 3,
  byrow = TRUE
)

product_sir

The net state changes are:
S + I -> 2 I    [-1, +1,  0]
I -> R          [ 0, -1, +1]


Run the simulation

result_sir <- jsf_simulate(
  x0 = c(S = N - 10, I = 10, R = 0),
  rates = rates_sir,
  reactant = reactant_sir,
  product = product_sir,
  do_disc = c(0, 1, 0),
  t_max = 60,
  dt = 0.1,
  switching_threshold = c(N, 10, N),
  species_names = c("S", "I", "R"),
  return_type = "JSFResult"
)

In this example, do_disc = c(0, 1, 0) allows the infectious compartment to be treated discretely when required.
This is useful because stochastic effects can be particularly important when the number of infectious individuals is small.


Inspect the result
Print the result:

result_sir

Calculate a summary:

summary(result_sir)

Plot the simulated trajectories:

plot(result_sir)

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
Return a data frame
The default output from jsf_simulate() is a regular R data.frame.

df_lv <- jsf_simulate(
  x0 = c(prey = 50, predator = 10),
  rates = rates_lv,
  reactant = reactant_lv,
  product = product_lv,
  do_disc = c(1, 1),
  t_max = 10,
  dt = 0.01,
  switching_threshold = c(30, 30),
  species_names = c("prey", "predator"),
  return_type = "data.frame"
)

head(df_lv)

A data frame returned by jsf_simulate() contains:

a time column; and
one column for each model species.

A data frame can later be converted into a JSFResult object:

result_from_df <- as_jsf_result(
  df_lv,
  method = "operator-splitting",
  config = list(
    model = "Lotka-Volterra",
    dt = 0.01,
    switching_threshold = c(30, 30)
  )
)

result_from_df

title: Getting started with rjsf
text:
Summary
The main rjsf workflow is:
Define the initial state
  -> define the rate function
  -> define the reactant and product matrices
  -> call jsf_simulate()
  -> return a data.frame or JSFResult
  -> inspect the output with print(), summary(), and plot()
Use a data.frame when you primarily need the simulation values for further analysis.
Use a JSFResult when you want a structured object containing both the simulation trajectories and their associated metadata.
